segments.text: How would you say I have canceled? I have canceled.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He cancelado. And we said that the version of the verb that you get after haber, you can use it like an adjective as well in Spanish, just as we do in English. For example, in English we could say it's canceled. We use the same version canceled that comes after haber, so we can do the same in Spanish. So how would you say it is canceled? And I remind you that the adjectives that we form in this way tend to go with estar, only with a few exceptions that are more flexible. So it is canceled?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está cancelado. What if we meant la fiesta, the party?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Está cancelada. Fiesta, by the way, is actually related to festival, festivity. We can see the e splitting between festival and fiesta. To complicate in Spanish, what's complication?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you want to say it has got complicated, it has got complicated, how do you think you will say it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Se ha complicado. It has got complicated, it has complicated itself we would say, very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Complicado, good. So you can say it is complicated...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está complicado. Actually, with this one you can use either. There tends to be a tendency to go with estar with these types of adjectives, but with complicado you could say either es complicado, está complicado, depending on what you are talking about. You might feel more drawn to one or to the other, but most of the time they're going to be interchangeable here. We can also make structures like should have, could have with this haber. Let's start with should have. Now should, we take it from the verb to owe, which also we use like must, and it's related to English debt.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Deber. Deber, good. So deber is to owe or must, and if you say would owe, you get should. So how would you say I should?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So now we can say I should have canceled, and this have is to have. I should to have canceled.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. I should have canceled, debería haber cancelado. I should have canceled it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Lo debería haber cancelado. Where else could that lo go there?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It's a- It's after the unchanged verb, so debería haberlo cancelado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, debería haberlo cancelado. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was could? So we take to be able and we say would be able to get this could, this could that refers to future. So what is to be able? Related to power.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Poder, good. So how would you say I would be able or I could?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Podría. So you could say something like I could have gone. I could have gone. What was to go?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ir. And what was gone, the version of to go after haber?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Aha. Podría haber ido. We could have gone. We could have gone.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Podríamos haber ido, good. So after haber, any version of haber, whether it's the to form, haber, whether it's habría, any version of haber is going to have -ado or -ido with the following verb. But some verbs are irregular, and they don't form their version after haber in this way. So to break, related to rupture in English, was romper. Now this after haber is not rompido. Rompido doesn't exist. It's irregular. After haber it's roto, r-o-t-o, roto. So how would you say I have broken it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo he roto. I have broken them?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Los he roto. What if you want to say it has broken? It has broken.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Se ha roto. It has broken itself, it has broken, very good. If you had just said ha roto, I would understand he, she, it, or you formal has or have broken, and I would be waiting to hear what was broken. So we have roto instead of rompido, let's say. Roto is the version of romper after haber, which means it will also count for the adjective. So if you want to say it is broken, how would you say it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está roto. And if it was a feminine thing?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está rota. To die is morir. Morir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And the version after haber is not morido, it's muerto. Muerto. How would you say he has died?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ha muerto. And with morir you can hear it with se or without se. There's not really a lot of difference. Sometimes the se doesn't actually make a lot of difference: ha muerto, se ha muerto, you hear both. Now if you want to say he is dead, how do you think you would say it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: You mean as if it's estar or ser?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We know that this type of adjective tends to go with...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well estar, but I could see why this specific one could also go with ser under certain circumstances.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, but it doesn't. It never goes with ser. So some of these adjectives we form in this way can go with ser, but this one can't. So firstly how would that be, he is dead?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está muerto. So complicado, for example, could go with ser and estar, but muerto can't. Maybe it's not just because they are this type of adjective that dead will go with estar, maybe it is about the way Spanish perceives the world. To be dead is a state that the soul goes through, let's say. You don't know what is the the perception behind that, or if it's just going with estar because it's one of these adjectives. So they're interesting points to think about, and thinking about those points helps your memory, even if you're just looking out of interest and not coming to any conclusions. How would you say I'm dead, and you can use this to mean tired, huh? This is quite common in Spanish. If you're really tired you can say, oh I'm dead.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Feminine: estoy muerta, good. You can say also I die myself, here like morirse, in all different kinds of circumstances: when something's really funny, when you can't believe something. In many different circumstances you could use that, you'll hear it around. But let's build it, let's see how it would sound. So to die, morir, I die myself, making this reflexive structure, how would it sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It's irregular, so the mue is going to come in. Muero, maybe, muero?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me muero, good. Me muero. So you will hear this all the time actually in Spanish, ¡Ay, me muero! Maybe from embarrassment, maybe from laughter, maybe from disbelief. It's a common thing: me muero. To open in Spanish is abrir. Abrir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Abrir. And if you want to say I have opened it, you say lo he abierto. So we don't have abrido, after haber we have abierto, another irregular one: lo he abierto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No. Good question though. Good that you're thinking about that. Abrir is a-b-r-i-r. Abrir becomes abierto. So how would you say it is open?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Está abierto. How would you say they are open?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Decir and hacer, to say or to tell, decir, and to make or to do, hacer, also are irregular after haber. These two verbs are quite irregular in most places, we will pay them a little more attention later. So decir to say or to tell and hacer to do and to make are irregular after haber. Decir becomes dicho, dicho, and hacer becomes hecho, which is why they're nice to see together because they both have this ch sound. Decir becomes dicho and hacer becomes hecho. So how would you say I have said it? I have said it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo he dicho. And what if you wanted to say I have told him?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But what we want here is not him, what we want here is to him. I have told to him.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le he dicho. Good. We have told him?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le hemos dicho, good. Interestingly dicho is also a noun. We said that some version of the verb can form the noun, sometimes it's the to form, sometimes it's the I form, sometimes it's the he/she/it form. Here it's this form. Un dicho is a saying. A saying. Hacer after haber becomes hecho. So how would you say I have done it or I have made it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo he hecho. I should have done it. I should have done it. I should...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. Debería haberlo hecho. Of course we can put the lo there because we have haber in the to form. Debería haberlo hecho or lo debería haber hecho, very good. You should have done it, informally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Deberías haberlo hecho. How would you say it is done? It is done.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Está hecho. You might also see this used like hecho en China, made in China, or hecho en España, made in Spain. You will see this on products, should be a nice reminder. So hecho as an adjective, made or done, no? Está hecho, it is done, it is made. But it can also be a noun: un hecho. Un hecho is a fact. And it's actually connected to the word fact, even though they look so different. There is in Spanish and English what we can call a kind of gray area between h's and f's, because in a phonetic change that occurred in Spanish, many f's became silent h's. Just as hecho is from hacer, fact is from to do. So faire, like in French if you know some French, is to do. And fact is related to faire, just as hecho is related to hacer. And we can find some other connections between this f and this silent h between English and Spanish. For example, in English we have fable. A fable is a story, and a story is spoken. And from there we see the relation with hablar, fable, hablar. We have fugitive, which is the same root as huir, h-u-i-r, huir, which means to escape or to run away in Spanish. We have hermano or hermana in Spanish, brother or sister, spelled h-e-r-m-a-n-o or with an a on the end for hermana, and there we see the connection with fraternal. Hembra, which means female, h-e-m-b-r-a. Even within Spanish you can see this phenomenon of the h's and the f's. For example, you have iron which is hierro, h-i-e-r-r-o, hierro, iron, and then you get ferrocarril which means railways. So they look totally unrelated, but if you know that the f became a silent h and that the e split into ie, you can see the connection between hierro and ferrocarril. You have profundo, profundo, profound in Spanish as you do in English, and then you have hondo which means deep. So hondo is the fundo bit of profundo, but with some changes: hondo, h-o-n-d-o, to mean deep. Fumar means to smoke, and then humo, h-u-m-o, is smoke, like a noun, el humo, the smoke. So there is some interesting things we can find between English and Spanish and within Spanish itself with these f's and h's. Also you can look out for some connections with other letters. You will find other pairs of letters like this, for example w's and g's: you get war in English and guerra in Spanish, William in English and Guillermo in Spanish. So this is an interesting thing to keep an eye out for to make connections between vocabulary, and of course in this way aids your memory.
